h1:
Bangkok Photo Itinerary
Made for Your Feed
intro: You can shoot good photos almost anywhere in Bangkok, but if you want a feed that actually hangs together, you have to order your stops so the light lands right. We've built this as two full days, starting with the temple that has the prettiest ceiling in the city, then street-art alleys by the river, cafes where every corner photographs well, and a rooftop sunset to close out each day. Every spot here has been checked to confirm it's still open, with suggested times and the angles everyone shoots.

blocks.html: What makes Bangkok fun for photographers is that you can mix it all into one day. Shoot a gilded temple in the morning, wander an old lane full of graffiti and faded Chinese signs by late morning, sit in a pastel cafe in the afternoon, then go up a tall tower at dusk for the skyline. The key is the order, not the number of stops. So we've matched each pocket of light to the right place: clear morning skies for temples, harsh afternoon sun spent indoors at cafes, and the golden hour saved for the rooftop.

blocks.text: Before you head out — so the day runs smooth

items: Dress so you can enter temples — most temples ask for sleeves and trousers or a skirt that covers the knees. Plain solid colours photograph more easily than busy patterns. Carry a shawl just in case.
Hit temples early — before 9am the crowds are still thin, you get clear angles and soft light, and you won't have to queue for a shot.
Bring a power bank — shooting all day drains your battery fast, especially if you're filming reels too.
Book the rooftop or arrive before 6pm — sunset-view tables fill quickly between 6 and 7pm, so arriving early gets you a better seat. Most places ask for smart casual — no shorts or flip-flops.
Get around by MRT/BTS + boat — traffic eats into your shooting time. The Blue Line and the Chao Phraya express boat can reach almost every stop in this plan.

blocks.text: Day 1 — emerald temple + Talad Noi + Old Town rooftop

blocks.html: Day one leads with the showstopper. The emerald-green ceiling at Wat Paknam is the shot that makes people ask where it was taken. After that, wander Talad Noi, which has graffiti, Chinese neon signs, and vintage cafes all in one neighbourhood. Close the day on a riverside rooftop in the Old Town.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Emerald temple → Talad Noi → riverside rooftop

items.activity: Wat Paknam Phasi Charoen — the emerald-green glass stupa ceiling
items.note: Go up to the 5th floor of the Maha Rajamongkol pagoda, where a green glass stupa stands roughly 8 metres tall beneath a blue cosmos-themed ceiling with 28 Buddha images. Open 08:00–18:00, free entry. Arrive early for fewer people; the light is best around 09:00–11:00.

items.activity: Take a boat or taxi to the Charoenkrung side and into Talad Noi
items.note: Get off at MRT Hua Lamphong and walk, or take a cross-river ferry over to the Yaowarat–Charoenkrung side.

items.activity: Walk Talad Noi — street art + old Chinese signs + riverside lanes
items.note: An old neighbourhood of shophouses mixing Chinese and European styles, with graffiti from artists like Alex Face scattered through the lanes. Popular shots include the old car turned into a planter, the Joe Sue Kong shrine, and Soi Wanit 2 along the river.

items.activity: Lunch at a local spot + a vintage cafe in Talad Noi
items.note: The little shops in the area photograph well from any angle. Coffee starts around ฿70–120, and it doubles as a break from the afternoon heat.

items.activity: Warehouse 30 / Charoenkrung Soi 30 — a renovated old warehouse
items.note: Old warehouses turned into a design space with shops, decor stores, and cafes. The bare concrete walls and steel frames photograph really well, and it's an easy walk on from Talad Noi.

items.activity: Head up an Old Town rooftop for sunset
items.note: The Old Town has wallet-friendly rooftops — drinks start around ฿220–250, beer ฿110–120. Arrive before 6pm for the view over Wat Arun and the river as the sky changes colour.

blocks.title: Shooting Wat Paknam
blocks.html: The ceiling is high up, so if you want both the glass stupa and the ceiling in one frame, lie on your back and shoot upward, or switch your phone to ultra-wide. Take your shoes off before going in. In the late morning, light from the ceiling openings makes the glass stupa glow at its best.

blocks.text: Day 2 — pastel cafes + flower market + downtown rooftop

blocks.html: Day two leans into cafes and colour. Start at a flower cafe above Pak Khlong Talat, work your way to a scent-themed cafe on the Sukhumvit side, then finish on a downtown rooftop that takes in the full skyscraper skyline.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Flower cafe → flower market → scent cafe → Siam rooftop

items.activity: Floral Cafe at Napasorn — a flower cafe above a florist
items.note: On the 2nd floor of a flower shop, decorated with fresh blooms that change with the season. The menu is flower-themed — rose ice cream, lavender tea, lemon cake. It's on Chakraphet Road, near Pak Khlong Talat.

items.activity: Walk Pak Khlong Talat — Bangkok's largest flower market
items.note: Heaps of marigolds, roses, and jasmine make for vivid, fun backdrops. It's open all day, but the selection peaks in the morning. Walk straight over from the flower cafe.

items.activity: Take the MRT to the Sukhumvit side for lunch
items.note: From Sanam Chai/Sam Yot, the Blue Line runs straight to Sukhumvit.

items.activity: Karmakamet Diner — a scent-themed cafe with a vintage herb garden
items.note: Vintage decor with an herb-garden corner and house scents, plus herb-infused drinks. It's a few minutes' walk from MRT Sukhumvit and makes a good indoor spot to dodge the afternoon heat.

items.activity: Go up a downtown rooftop for the skyline + sunset
items.note: Plenty of options here, like Octave atop the Marriott Sukhumvit (open-air across floors 45–49, cocktails around ฿400–450, happy hour 17:00–19:00 at 50% off), or CRU Champagne Bar on the 59th floor of Centara Grand at CentralWorld with 360-degree views (smart casual, no entry under 20).

items.activity: Catch the blue hour + city lights
items.note: About 20–30 minutes after sunset is blue hour, when the deep blue sky plays off the building lights — the best window of the day for skyline shots.

blocks.title: Rooftop tips
blocks.html: On a tight budget, go during happy hour (many spots run roughly 17:00–19:00) — you get both better prices and the golden-hour light at once. A single drink is usually enough to hold a view table. Check the dress code before you go; many places say no shorts or flip-flops.

blocks.text: Backup photo spots — if you have extra time

items.name: Wat Arun
items.blurb: A porcelain-tiled prang on the Chao Phraya, best at early dawn and just before sunset. Shoot from the opposite bank to get the whole prang in frame.

items.name: Wat Benchamabophit
items.blurb: The white marble temple in a Thai-meets-Western style, with marble imported from Italy. Early morning light through the fretwork reflects beautifully off the white walls.

items.name: Erawan Museum
items.blurb: A giant three-headed elephant over a pastel-pink building. Inside there's a spiral staircase with stained glass and a glowing dome that looks straight out of a film. It's in Samut Prakan, reachable by BTS.

items.name: Soi Nana, Yaowarat
items.blurb: A lane of stylish bars and cafes in Chinatown. At night the neon signs and old buildings photograph really well — a good follow-on from Talad Noi in the evening.

items: Entry fees — Wat Paknam is free, Wat Arun is ฿200 (foreigners), and Pak Khlong Talat and Talad Noi are free to wander.
Cafes — drink + a snack runs around ฿150–350 per stop.
Rooftops — drinks start around ฿220 in the Old Town and reach ฿400–1,000 at the luxury towers. Check prices before you order.
Transit — MRT/BTS is ฿17–62 per trip, the Chao Phraya express boat ฿16–34; a full day adds up to only a few hundred baht.
Total per day — photos + cafes + a budget rooftop runs around ฿700–1,200 per person; add more if you go for a luxury rooftop, depending on the drinks.

blocks.html: To keep things easy on yourself, book a stay near the river or close to the BTS/MRT so you can dart in and out of photo spots quickly without losing time to traffic — and you might land a city-view room to shoot yourself in the morning.

faq.q: Which Bangkok temple is the most Instagrammable?
faq.a: Wat Paknam Phasi Charoen is the hottest right now thanks to the emerald-green glass stupa ceiling on the 5th floor, which is almost impossible to find anywhere else. After that come Wat Arun on the Chao Phraya and the white marble Wat Benchamabophit. Visit all of them in the morning for thinner crowds and softer light.

faq.q: Where do you shoot in Talad Noi, and how do you get there?
faq.a: Talad Noi sits in the Charoenkrung area next to Chinatown. The popular shots are the old car turned into a planter, the old shrines, the Chinese neon signs, and the riverside lane Soi Wanit 2. The easiest way in is MRT to Hua Lamphong and then a short walk, or a cross-river ferry to the Yaowarat side. The whole neighbourhood is free to explore.

faq.q: How much do Bangkok rooftops cost, and what should you wear?
faq.a: Drinks start around ฿220–250 at Old Town rooftops, while at luxury towers like Octave or CRU cocktails run roughly ฿400–1,000. Many places ask for smart casual with no shorts or flip-flops, and some don't admit anyone under 20. Arrive before 6pm to grab a sunset-view table.

faq.q: How many days do you need for a Bangkok photo trip?
faq.a: Two days is about right. Day one covers the emerald temple and Talad Noi on the Old Town side; day two focuses on cafes and the skyline on the newer side of the city. With only one day, do Wat Paknam in the morning, Talad Noi in the afternoon, and finish at a rooftop in the evening.

faq.q: What time of day is best for photos in Bangkok?
faq.a: Temples shoot best in the morning, 08:00–11:00, when crowds are thin and the light is soft. Cafes suit the harsh-sun afternoon since they're indoors. Save rooftops and the skyline for the golden hour before sunset, around 17:30–18:30, then carry on into the blue hour for another 20–30 minutes after the sun drops.
